report:
Summary
- There is a clear, focused difference: it is concentrated overwhelmingly at token-position 0 across almost all layers. That pattern is most consistent with a changed beginning-of-sequence residual — e.g., a different BOS token embedding, a persistent learned prefix, or a different prepended system prompt.
- The semantic directions (logit-lens top tokens for those high‑norm cells) shift the model toward negative/urgent/news/medical/legal vocabulary and imperative/check words. Examples from deeper layers: tragic, tragedy, law, surgeon, clinic, surgery, downturn, curse, shocked, blitz, rescue, Do/Check/ensure. Mid layers show words like rejected/normal/human/relevant/Every/Stay as well.
- Put together, the evidence suggests Model B (relative to A) has an added/modified start-of-sequence bias that steers generations toward an urgent/negative-news or medical/legal framing and toward imperative/checking language.

How I reached this
- The L2-norms show almost all of the difference mass sits at pos0 (and to a lesser extent pos1 in deeper layers). That is the canonical sign of a persistent prefix or modified BOS embedding rather than a localized behavioral change later in the token stream.
- The logit-lens decoding of the high-norm pos0 cells transforms from concrete nouns in early layers to consistent high-level tokens in later layers that cluster around “tragic / law / surgeon / clinic / rescue / shocked / downturn / Do / Check / ensure” — i.e., words you’d see in reporting of incidents, emergencies, legal/medical contexts, or instruction-like safety phrasing.
- That pattern is what you’d expect if one checkpoint had been fine-tuned or conditioned with a prefix emphasizing news/incident/medical/legal/safety style, or if a policy/safety prompt had been prepended.

Caveats
- The evidence is consistent with a changed prefix/BOS embedding that biases topic/style, but it does not uniquely prove why (e.g., dataset shift vs. explicit safety fine-tune vs. an inserted system prompt). The logit-lens tokens are noisy and varied at early layers, so the precise semantic intent should be validated by observing full-model generations under controlled prompts (patchscope continuations or direct sampling).
- I cannot (and am not) claiming a particular named fine‑tuning objective beyond “biasing initial context toward urgent/negative/medical/legal/instructional vocabulary,” because the data support that higher‑level characterization but not a unique training cause.
